query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of titanium (Ti) to the equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion and subtle microstructural modifications without compromising its high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy known for excellent high-temperature (≈1600 °C) performance but very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of Ti (on the order of 5–10 atomic %) to the NbMoTaW composition to form a (NbMoTaW)1−xTix alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests at room temperature to assess ductility, compression/tensile tests at around 1600 °C for high-temperature performance, and ion irradiation experiments (or equivalent irradiation simulation) to evaluate radiation resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion and possibly the formation of finely dispersed, subtle secondary features (e.g., slight ordering or nano-precipitates) within the BCC matrix, which help mediate dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Ti’s incorporation is expected to reduce interfacial decohesion by strengthening the grain boundaries via altered atomic bonding and local lattice distortions. This facilitates easier dislocation slip at lower temperatures while preserving the robust BCC framework that underpins high-temperature yield strength and the defect recombination characteristics contributing to irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped NbMoTaW baseline, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit improved room-temperature ductility (i.e. higher plastic strain prior to fracture), while retaining a yield strength near that of the baseline at 1600 °C and showing similar levels of irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW with poor room-temperature ductility, high compressive/tensile strength at 1600 °C, and irradiation resistance as predicted from first-principles calculations.
generation.boundary: The Ti content must remain low (e.g., ≤10 at%) because excessive Ti could trigger unwanted phase transformations or precipitate formations that might reduce high-temperature strength or alter irradiation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Ti concentration and the complete influence on high-temperature deformation mechanisms remain uncertain until validated by systematic experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys by arc melting and appropriate thermal treatment that include the baseline NbMoTaW and versions with 0, 5, and 10 at% Ti. Characterize their microstructures using XRD and TEM. Conduct room temperature tensile/compression tests, high-temperature (≈1600 °C) mechanical testing, and subject samples to controlled ion irradiation followed by microstructural and hardness evaluations.
measurements: Room temperature plastic strain and yield stress
High-temperature yield strength and softening resistance at 1600 °C
Irradiation-induced defect density and hardness changes
Microstructural phase analysis and grain boundary evaluation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the addition of Ti does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility, or if it results in a measurable degradation of high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance compared to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
